newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic deals partial defeat to hardliners.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic deals partial defeat to hardliners.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic's recognition on Friday of opposition election victories in Serbia deals a partial defeat to hardliners who want to retrench socialist rule behind a siege economy, diplomats said.
Serbia told the OSCE the opposition won in nine Belgrade municipalities but did not mention ceding control of the city council. It also left the future of other disputed towns in question.

"Milosevic made a move to conciliate the West but it's not enough," one Western envoy said. "We'll have to see what happens in the other places where the opposition got majorities before being sure which way he has swung."
The United States and other Western governments have backed the Zajedno (Together) opposition's claim to have won Belgrade and 14 other big towns in the local elections in November 17.

Milosevic's indecisive handling of six weeks of opposition protests against election fraud has stemmed partly from a fierce internal battle between hardliners and reformers in his Socialist party (SPS) leadership.
Signs have grown that moderates are slowly prevailing with their argument that Serbia faces economic ruin and even greater social conflict if the SPS refuses to slacken its 50-year grip on power.
But the gaps in Milosevic's admission to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) indicate the party struggle is not over.
Diplomats speculated some results have been left open to provide a pretext for a re-run of the elections.
A senior foreign ministry official primed OSCE envoys this week with expectations of a compromise that meant an historic defeat for the hardliners' goal of maintaining one-party rule.
Other promising signals included a government pledge to begin privatisation of the economy's huge state sector and a denunciation of election fraud by the Serbian Orthodox Church.
The church has never hidden its distaste for Milosevic. But its support will be valuable to him if he now opts for conciliation as the best chance of his own political survival.

The OSCE has hinted that surrender on the election results could begin Serbia's rehabilitation after years of exclusion from international bodies including the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the OSCE itself.
Any return to the international arena would depend on democratic reforms by Milosevic without which he cannot rebuild an economy crippled by U.N. sanctions.
Reforms that would end the socialist monopoly of power are the hurdle at which the hardliners balk for fear of being called to account for the criminalisation of Serbian politics.
Political sources said hardliners favoured a siege Serbia, with full SPS authority restored, that would turn its back on the West and live on trade with Russia and China.
The question remains whether Serbia's impoverished population, having glimpsed socialist vulnerability, would tolerate a continued regime of privation.

The loyalty of the army and police, which the SPS relied on in the past to cow dissent, is no longer guaranteed. Dissident army officers warned Milosevic at the weekend that any military coup would be in support of democracy against the SPS.

Although Milosevic's political credibility has been badly damaged by the election fiasco, political sources said his position has been strengthened against the SPS hardliners by the OSCE escape route and the army officers' intervention.

The Serbian leader built his career in the old Yugoslav communist party but has been notoriously unideological in his pursuit of power, adapting his priorities smoothly to changes in political circumstances.

The dispute with Zajedno upset a scenario under which the SPS, which won Yugoslav federal elections in November, would consolidate its power for the foreseeable future at Serbian republican elections due by the end of 1997. It is no longer a certainty the SPS can win.
Milosevic appears to be still trying to persuade the hardliners their best hope lies in helping him to take over the federal presidency later this year.

The federal office, revamped with strong executive powers, would guarantee the SPS a bulwark against Zajedno even under a fair election system that let the opposition win the Serbian presidency or control of the Serbian parliament.
Milosevic would retain room for manoeuvre to gradually disengage from his hardliners and establish a new centre ground between SPS moderates and the opposition with whom he has flirted in the past.
